A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
P: 1. Obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type and screen; arrange emergency department evaluation today, vascular access and resuscitation as indicated, with gastroenterology consultation and endoscopy after stabilization. The known hemoglobin and melena already make a very-low-risk outpatient pathway inappropriate; calculate the complete bleeding risk assessment when missing values are available. A restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g/dL is commonly used in stable hospitalized upper-GI bleeding, but ongoing hemorrhage, instability and cardiovascular disease change decisions. Stop ibuprofen; discuss clinician-directed acid suppression and non-NSAID analgesia. Educate about black tarry stools, hematemesis, syncope and the immediate disposition.

2. Biopsy at the time of that same endoscopy, including the ulcer margin and the gastric antrum and body; gastroenterology consultation in hospital. Treat H. pylori if the biopsy or stool antigen is positive, avoiding amoxicillin for her penicillin allergy, which caused lip and facial swelling. Educate on what the endoscopy involves and why her mother's gastric cancer at 68 makes a tissue diagnosis important. Repeat endoscopy in 8 to 12 weeks to document that the ulcer has healed.

3. Ferritin, iron, total iron binding capacity and reticulocyte count; serial hemoglobin during the admission. Resume oral iron with vitamin C after the endoscopy and educate on taking it with food to limit nausea. OMT is deferred while she is bleeding; rib raising and paraspinal inhibition to T5-T9 may be offered once she is stable. Educate that the fatigue and the lightheadedness on standing are from blood loss and should improve as the ulcer heals.

ideal_encounter_extras: Ask about stool color explicitly. She will not volunteer the black stool - she has already explained it to herself as the iron tablets - and it is the single most important fact in the case.
Ask the dose and frequency of the ibuprofen, not just whether she takes 'anything for pain'. This medication exposure is relevant to the assessment, but it does not establish a diagnosis.
Ask the allergy reaction, not just the allergen. 'Penicillin - swelling' rules out standard triple therapy; 'penicillin - upset stomach' would not.
Inspect the conjunctivae. It is thirty seconds and it converts 'she says she is tired' into a documented physical finding.
Auscultate before you percuss or palpate. The hyperactive bowel sounds are a real finding here, and palpating first changes them.

Rectal: Refused at this time.

A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
P: 1. Obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type and screen; arrange emergency department evaluation today, vascular access and resuscitation as indicated, with gastroenterology consultation and endoscopy after stabilization. The known hemoglobin and melena already make a very-low-risk outpatient pathway inappropriate; calculate the complete bleeding risk assessment when missing values are available. A restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g/dL is commonly used in stable hospitalized upper-GI bleeding, but ongoing hemorrhage, instability and cardiovascular disease change decisions. Stop ibuprofen; discuss clinician-directed acid suppression and non-NSAID analgesia. Educate about black tarry stools, hematemesis, syncope and the immediate disposition. Use plain language, pause between steps, and invite teach-back.

2. Biopsy at the time of that same endoscopy, including the ulcer margin and the gastric antrum and body; gastroenterology consultation in hospital. Treat H. pylori if the biopsy or stool antigen is positive, avoiding amoxicillin for her penicillin allergy, which caused lip and facial swelling. Educate on what the endoscopy involves and why her mother's gastric cancer at 68 makes a tissue diagnosis important. Repeat endoscopy in 8 to 12 weeks to document that the ulcer has healed.

3. Ferritin, iron, total iron binding capacity and reticulocyte count; serial hemoglobin during the admission. Resume oral iron with vitamin C after the endoscopy and educate on taking it with food to limit nausea. OMT is deferred while she is bleeding; rib raising and paraspinal inhibition to T5-T9 may be offered once she is stable. Educate that the fatigue and the lightheadedness on standing are from blood loss and should improve as the ulcer heals.

A: 1. NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
P: 1. Obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type and screen; arrange emergency department evaluation today, vascular access and resuscitation as indicated, with gastroenterology consultation and endoscopy after stabilization. The known hemoglobin and melena already make a very-low-risk outpatient pathway inappropriate; calculate the complete bleeding risk assessment when missing values are available. A restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g/dL is commonly used in stable hospitalized upper-GI bleeding, but ongoing hemorrhage, instability and cardiovascular disease change decisions. Stop ibuprofen; discuss clinician-directed acid suppression and non-NSAID analgesia. Educate about black tarry stools, hematemesis, syncope and the immediate disposition. Agree on a practical contact and transportation plan; verify the patient can describe the urgent warning signs.

2. Biopsy at the time of that same endoscopy, including the ulcer margin and the gastric antrum and body; gastroenterology consultation in hospital. Treat H. pylori if the biopsy or stool antigen is positive, avoiding amoxicillin for her penicillin allergy, which caused lip and facial swelling. Educate on what the endoscopy involves and why her mother's gastric cancer at 68 makes a tissue diagnosis important. Repeat endoscopy in 8 to 12 weeks to document that the ulcer has healed.

3. Ferritin, iron, total iron binding capacity and reticulocyte count; serial hemoglobin during the admission. Resume oral iron with vitamin C after the endoscopy and educate on taking it with food to limit nausea. OMT is deferred while she is bleeding; rib raising and paraspinal inhibition to T5-T9 may be offered once she is stable. Educate that the fatigue and the lightheadedness on standing are from blood loss and should improve as the ulcer heals.
